title: Did Zhuge Liang Anger Zhou Yu to Death? History Gave His Death at 36 Just Four Characters
description:
You've surely heard it: Zhuge Liang provoked Zhou Yu three times, and he cried "Heaven made Yu; why Liang?" and died. This episode follows the Records of the Three Kingdoms and sets his last journey beside the novel. In Jian'an 15 (210), Zhou Yu proposed to Sun Quan a plan to take Shu in the west, then turn back and hold Xiangyang; Sun Quan agreed. Zhou Yu went back to Jiangling to pack, set off, and died of illness at Baqiu, aged 36; the Biography of Zhou Yu says only "died ill at Baqiu". Earlier, at the Nanjun front, a stray arrow struck his right side; badly wounded, he returned to camp, yet got up to tour it, so Cao Ren withdrew. The history does not make that arrow the cause of death. The Biography of Lu Su records a memorial Zhou Yu sent when gravely ill, recommending Lu Su; Pei Songzhi's notes quote another, from the Jiangbiao Zhuan, that says he was "struck by sudden illness on the road". Pei Songzhi says the two "agree in meaning but differ in wording"; neither names the illness. Sun Quan mourned in plain white and met the coffin at Wuhu; Lu Su took over Zhou Yu's troops, and Cheng Pu became governor of Nanjun. The three provocations, Zhuge Liang's letter in Chapter 57 and the cry "Heaven made Yu; why Liang?" come from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

Where we draw the line: death by illness is on file; which illness, the records do not say. We do not diagnose him, and we do not call it an old wound reopening. Cheng Pu's "like drinking mellow wine" comes from the Jiangbiao Zhuan in Pei Songzhi's notes; it records his temperament and cannot prove Zhou Yu never got angry. Sources are listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone; scenes from the novel all show a book, to keep them apart from the histories.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten on 2026-10-25 under new guidelines)

zy101.text: You know it: Zhuge Liang kept angering Zhou Yu, who cried “Heaven made Yu; why Liang?” and died.

zy102.text: Yet the history of his life tells how he died in just four characters.

zy103.text: In 210, the 15th year of Jian'an, Zhou Yu pitched Sun Quan a march west.

zy104.text: Sun Quan agreed. Zhou Yu went back to Jiangling, packed, and set off.

zy105.text: But he himself only got as far as a place called Baqiu.

zy106.text: Earlier, at the Nanjun front, a stray arrow was already flying at him.

zy107.text: This file sets the Records of the Three Kingdoms, from Liyang to Baqiu, beside the novel's three provocations.

zy108.text: Did Zhuge Liang really anger Zhou Yu to death?

zy201.text: No wonder Sun Quan agreed: Zhou Yu's bond with the Sun family went back to Sun Ce.

zy202.text: Zhou Yu, Sun Ce's age, housed him in the big house south of the road, and bowed to Sun Ce's mother.

zy203.text: Later, set to cross east, Sun Ce wrote from Liyang; Zhou Yu led troops to meet him.

zy204.text: At 24, all of Wu already called him “Zhou Lang.”

zy205.text: The “Zhou Lang” you know is history, not the novel's coinage.

zy206.text: Sun Ce died; Zhou Yu marched home to mourn.

zy207.text: What would Zhou Yu do now?

zy208.text: He stayed as Protector of the Army, aiding, with Zhang Zhao, Jiangdong's new ruler Sun Quan.

zy209.text: Their bond went deeper than I'd first thought.

zy210.text: Then, in Jian'an 13, 208, Cao Cao's great army came down the river.

zy211.text: Liu Cong had surrendered, and Jingzhou's navy fell to Cao Cao.

zy301.text: Some of Sun Quan's men did urge surrender.

zy302.text: They said the Yangtze's natural barrier couldn't stop Cao's army now.

zy304.text: He said northern troops, new to boats and the south, would fall ill.

zy305.text: But it wasn't his idea alone: Pei Songzhi's notes point out Lu Su urged Sun Quan to resist even earlier.

zy306.text: So if you hear Red Cliffs was all Zhou Yu, take it with a grain of salt.

zy307.text: Zhou Yu sought 30,000 elite men to face Cao from Xiakou.

zy309.text: Zhou Yu, and the veteran Cheng Pu.

zy310.text: Remember Cheng Pu: he'll later say something delightful.

zy311.text: Red Cliffs, round one: Cao retreated north; Zhou Yu, south.

zy312.text: Huang Gai saw it: Cao's ships were linked bow to stern, and could be burned.

zy313.text: He filled boats with brushwood and oil, and first wrote Cao Cao feigning surrender.

zy314.text: Each big ship towed a small boat for escape.

zy316.text: All the way to the camps ashore.

zy317.text: You know the fire at Red Cliffs; in the histories, it was Huang Gai's idea.

zy318.text: I always feel he's the real star of that fire.

zy319.text: I also think this battle is why Sun Quan later dared send Zhou Yu west.

zy320.text: Cao Cao then headed north, but left Cao Ren at Jiangling.

zy321.text: How would Zhou Yu pull the Jiangling thorn?

zy401.text: At first he faced Cao Ren across the river; neither made a move.

zy402.text: The Wu Lu in Pei's notes says Cao Ren's Jiangling had lots of grain.

zy403.text: Say you're Zhou Yu: the city has grain, so waiting won't work.

zy404.text: Gan Ning went to Yiling; Cao Ren besieged him.

zy406.text: Leaving a rear guard, he led the rescue.

zy407.text: Siege lifted, he crossed and camped north.

zy408.text: Both sides set a battle; Zhou Yu himself rode to the front.

zy409.text: That stray arrow hit his right side.

zy410.text: The Records call it severe; he had to go back to camp.

zy411.text: Hearing Zhou Yu was bedridden, Cao Ren drew up for battle.

zy412.text: Badly wounded, could Zhou Yu get up?

zy414.text: He toured the camp, rallying his men.

zy416.text: Reading this, I was really nervous for him.

zy417.text: Sun Quan made him a general and governor of Nanjun.

zy418.text: But could this arrow be what later killed him?

zy419.text: Then, based at Jiangling, he kept advising Sun Quan.

zy420.text: But Jingzhou now held another man; how would Zhou Yu handle him?

zy501.text: That man was Liu Bei, now governor of Jingzhou as General of the Left.

zy502.text: Liu Bei met Sun Quan, and Zhou Yu then sent in a memorial.

zy503.text: He said: keep Liu Bei in Wu, and split up his two great generals, each to a different post.

zy504.text: You can tell: it stops Liu Bei going back to lead troops.

zy506.text: No. Cao Cao still loomed north, and Liu Bei seemed hard to control.

zy507.text: Here the record has just two judgments, not Zhou Yu's anger.

zy508.text: If anything, I find this Zhou Yu more like a man at work.

zy509.text: Then he sent a second: the westward plan from the start.

zy510.text: Yizhou's Liu Zhang was pressed hard by Zhang Lu.

zy511.text: Zhou Yu figured Cao, just beaten, couldn't fight Jiangdong yet.

zy512.text: So how did he plan to go?

zy513.text: He'd march west with General Sun Yu,

zy514.text: take Shu, then deal with Zhang Lu;

zy515.text: and leave that general to hold it.

zy516.text: He'd return to hold Xiangyang with Sun Quan, pressing north on Cao.

zy517.text: Draw this line in your head: west first, then north, one big loop.

zy518.text: Honestly, that map's ambition startled me the first time.

zy519.text: This time Sun Quan said yes.

zy520.text: That brings us to the opening: he went back to Jiangling, packed, and set off.

zy521.text: What on earth stopped him on the way?

zy601.text: It was illness. The Biography of Lu Su says Zhou Yu was gravely ill.

zy602.text: Ill, he wrote to Sun Quan.

zy603.text: What would a man that ill write?

zy604.text: It opens with the realm still at war, a worry he carried day and night.

zy605.text: He urged Sun Quan to plan for dangers ahead.

zy607.text: Cao Cao still a foe, Liu Bei near at Gong'an,

zy608.text: and the people here not yet won over.

zy609.text: Notice? Up to here, he hasn't said a word about his own illness.

zy610.text: Then he named one man: “Lu Su has the wits to replace me.”

zy611.text: Lu Su was no surprise; Zhou Yu had recommended him to Sun Quan early on.

zy612.text: Only at the end did he mention the day he would fall.

zy613.text: Reading this, I'm a bit lost for words.

zy614.text: That's not all: Pei Songzhi's notes, quoting the Jiangbiao Zhuan, keep a second letter.

zy615.text: It says he fell suddenly ill on the road, treated himself, but got no better.

zy616.text: It also says: everyone dies; a long or short life isn't worth regretting.

zy617.text: What he truly regretted was the grand plan left undone.

zy618.text: Pei Songzhi notes: both letters mean the same, worded differently.

zy619.text: Do the letters say what illness it was?

zy620.text: No. Whichever one you read, the illness goes unnamed.

zy621.text: In the Biography of Zhou Yu, those four: died ill at Baqiu.

zy623.text: Pei Songzhi takes care to note: this Baqiu where he died

zy624.text: and the Baqiu he once guarded share a name, not a place.

zy625.text: Even ancient scholars feared a mix-up.

zy627.text: The Biography of Zhou Yu has it, not as the cause of death.

zy628.text: So “his old wound reopened” is a guess; the record doesn't have it.

zy629.text: What would Sun Quan do at the news?

zy701.text: Sun Quan mourned him in plain white, and all around him grieved too.

zy702.text: As the coffin returned to Wu, Sun Quan met it at Wuhu himself.

zy703.text: Sun Quan paid all the costs on the way.

zy704.text: Jiangbiao Zhuan quotes Sun Quan: Zhou Yu could aid a king;

zy705.text: now he dies so young; whom can I rely on?

zy706.text: As Sun Quan, you'd likely worry first: who takes Zhou Yu's troops?

zy707.text: To Lu Su, as the letter asked?

zy708.text: And the man who took over Zhou Yu's troops was Lu Su: Sun Quan made him a colonel.

zy709.text: Over 4,000 of Zhou Yu's men and his four fief counties went to Lu Su.

zy710.text: Cheng Pu got to govern Nanjun.

zy711.text: Reading this, I thought: someone took his last letter seriously.

zy712.text: But in the later novel, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, his last road differs.

zy713.text: In the novel, who catches up?

zy801.text: It's a letter from Zhuge Liang that catches up.

zy802.text: But before it arrives, the novel has twice angered him.

zy803.text: Chapter 51 also uses the Nanjun arrow wound: Zhou Yu's plan fails, and the wound bursts open.

zy804.text: Next, for Sun Quan, he plots a marriage ruse,

zy805.text: but Liu Bei escapes with Lady Sun: provocation two.

zy806.text: If you binge series, you can guess: a third is coming.

zy807.text: Chapter 56's title says it: the third provocation.

zy808.text: In Chapter 57, Zhuge Liang sends a letter.

zy810.text: The letter in the novel: Yizhou has strong people, rugged land, long supply lines;

zy811.text: weak as Liu Zhang is, he can hold it.

zy812.text: The sharpest point comes last: Cao Cao hasn't forgotten Red Cliffs; if Jiangdong empties, he may pounce.

zy813.text: Honestly, the letter makes a lot of sense.

zy814.text: In the novel, Zhou Yu reads it and sighs deeply.

zy815.text: He writes Sun Quan first, then tells his officers: serve the Marquis of Wu, finish the task.

zy816.text: Then he faints; that cry, “Heaven made Yu; why Liang?”, comes after he wakes.

zy817.text: So is that line in the histories?

zy819.text: Nor do checkable surviving texts blame Zhuge Liang for his illness.

zy820.text: So was the Zhou Yu of the histories easily angered?

zy821.text: The Biography of Zhou Yu: generous, well liked, clashing only with Cheng Pu.

zy822.text: His Red Cliffs co-commander. The Jiangbiao Zhuan says

zy823.text: Cheng Pu used his age to bully him many times;

zy824.text: Zhou Yu stayed humble, never settling scores.

zy825.text: Later Cheng Pu said: befriending Zhou Yu is like drinking mellow wine; you get drunk without noticing.

zy826.text: Could you stand an elder like that?

zy828.text: I feel he's not quite the same man as the novel's oft-angered Zhou Yu;

zy829.text: But it's a record of temperament; it can't prove he never got angry.

zy830.text: So, did Zhuge Liang anger Zhou Yu to death?

zy831.text: This case: three provocations, filed as fiction; the illness, unsolved.

zy832.text: Always riled by someone? Comment your comeback.

zy833.text: This channel sticks to the records; subscribe to open files with me.
